When destination demand shocks are constructed from shift-share instruments—such as visitor origin countries $\times$ seasonal travel shifters—non-random exposure across commercial hubs propagates through the urban network $(I - M)^{-1}$. Following Borusyak and Hull (2023) and Allen et al. (2026), `build_exposures(design = "shift_share")` propagates expected shifters through the exact same network operator $(I - M)^{-1}$ so `estimate_bilateral()` automatically controls for predictable network exposure.

```{r}
library(urbanwelfare)

sim <- sim_urban_city(N = 50, T = 8, seed = 101)
acct <- urban_account(sim$E_R0, sim$H_0, sim$origins, sim$destinations)

# Build shift-share network exposures + Borusyak-Hull propagated expected controls
exp_ss <- build_exposures(
  account     = acct,
  shock_panel = sim$shift_share,
  design      = "shift_share"
)
summary(exp_ss)

# Inspect Rotemberg instrument relevance weights across visitor origin groups
rot <- rotemberg_weights(exp_ss, acct)
print(rot)
cat("Effective shock count (1 / HHI):", round(attr(rot, "effective_shocks_hhi_inv"), 2), "\n")
```

## Robustness Extensions: CES Shopping Residuals, Workplace Mobility, & Finite Bounds

`urbanwelfare` provides pipe-friendly extensions relaxing fixed shopping amenities, fixed workplaces, and first-order log-linearization while holding the estimated bilateral responses fixed:

```{r}
fit_ss <- estimate_bilateral(sim$bilateral_panel, exp_ss)
welf_ext <- recover_welfare(fit_ss, acct, se_method = "none") |>
  add_shopping_wedge(sigma = c(2.0, 3.456, 8.235)) |>
  add_workplace_mobility(eps = 3.3) |>
  add_finite_bounds(sigma_ces = 3.456)

welf_ext$extensions$shopping_wedge$summary
welf_ext$extensions$workplace_mobility$summary
welf_ext$extensions$finite_bounds$summary
```
